title: Date and occasion
short: Published in Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845), not 1842; Browning said it records no historical event.
body: The poem appeared in Bells and Pomegranates VII, Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845); the archive's '1842' label confuses it with Dramatic Lyrics. Browning later wrote that 'There is no historical incident whatever commemorated in the poem': he meant it as a general impression of the sieges and warfare of the Low Countries. He is said to have written it at sea, on the voyage to Italy in 1838, seven years before it was printed. Despite the disclaimer, an editor suggested the Pacification of Ghent (1576), the alliance of the Netherlands provinces against Spain, as a possible background. The 'news' is never stated.

title: Galloping metre
short: Rhymed couplets of four-stress anapaestic lines (two unstressed beats before each stress) imitate the rhythm of hooves.
body: Each line has four main stresses with mostly two unstressed syllables before each ('I GALloped, DIRCK GALloped, we GALloped all THREE'), the rhythm known as anapaestic tetrameter. The couplets rush forward, and the repeated 'galloped' supplies onomatopoeia. Browning varies the beat with sudden stops ('So Joris broke silence'), spondees, and heavy consonants in passages of exhaustion. The six-line stanza groupings are irregular in sense, and some run over. Commentators have praised the poem as one of the great English imitations of motion in verse; it was much recited in schools.

title: the watch; gate-bolts; postern
short: The night-guard of Ghent opens the gate for the riders; a 'postern' is a back or side gate in a city wall.
body: The opening places us inside a walled city at night: the 'watch' (town guard) wishes them 'Good speed!', the bolts are drawn ('undrew'), and the wall itself seems to echo 'Speed!' as the horses pass through. The 'postern' shuts behind them and 'the lights sank to rest'. The vocabulary is late-medieval or early modern and suits a vaguely sixteenth- or seventeenth-century Flanders. The three riders set off at midnight, moving into a darkness that will brighten through the stages of dawn and morning.

title: pique; girths; cheek-strap; bit
short: The rider adjusts his saddle and bridle while galloping; 'pique' is usually glossed as the peak (pommel) of the saddle.
body: The lines show expert horsemanship: tightening the saddle's 'girths' (the belly-straps), shortening the stirrups, setting the 'pique' right, rebuckling the 'cheek-strap' of the bridle, and letting the bit hang slacker so the horse can stretch its head. The meaning of 'pique' has puzzled readers; editors usually take it as a variant of 'peak', the raised front of the saddle, and it is one of the poem's few obscure words. The point is that all this is done at full gallop, 'Nor galloped less steadily Roland a whit', and without a word.

title: The route: Lokeren to Dalhem
short: The riders pass real towns in Flanders and Brabant: Lokeren, Boom, Düffel, Mechelen, Aarschot, Hasselt, Looz, Tongeren, Dalhem.
body: The stages run roughly from west to east across present-day Belgium, from Ghent to Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle) in Germany, well over a hundred miles. The towns are Lokeren, Boom, 'Düffeld' (Düffel), 'Mecheln' (Mechelen or Malines), 'Aershot' (Aarschot), Hasselt, Looz (Borgloon), Tongres (Tongeren) and Dalhem. The incident is invented, but the route is geographically plausible, and each town is linked to a moment of the night: cock-crow, a yellow star (the morning star) at Boom, morning at Düffeld, the half-chime of the great church-tower at Mechelen (St Rumbold's), sunrise at Aarschot. Time and space advance together.

title: a great yellow star
short: The morning star (probably Venus) rises before dawn; Browning personifies it as a spectator of the ride.
body: Personifications of watching nature recur: the star 'came out to see', the cattle at Aershot 'stood black' against the sun 'To stare through the mist at us', and later 'The broad sun above laughed a pitiless laugh'. The universe watches the riders but does not help them. The progression from moonset (l. 13) to star, morning, sunrise and full sun is carefully managed, and the sun's growing heat in the later stanzas accompanies the exhaustion of the horses.

title: Roland
short: The narrator's horse bears the name of Charlemagne's great paladin, the hero of the Chanson de Roland.
body: Roland, Charlemagne's nephew in the Old French epic, is the type of loyal, self-sacrificing heroism, and the name fits the horse who alone completes the ride. There is also a hint of the destination: Aix-la-Chapelle was Charlemagne's capital. The description of Roland in stanzas 4 and 5 is the poem's most vivid writing, with 'resolute shoulders' butting away the haze 'as some bluff river headland its spray' and one ear bent back for the rider's voice while 'the other pricked out on his track'. The eye's 'black intelligence', glancing 'O'er its white edge' at the rider, suggests a partnership between horse and man.

title: spume-flakes; aye and anon
short: 'Spume' is foam or froth; 'aye and anon' means continually and repeatedly.
body: Roland's lips throw 'spume-flakes' upward as he gallops, a sign of extreme exertion. 'Aye and anon' combines 'aye' (always) and 'anon' (again, presently), an archaic doublet emphasising repetition. The physical detail anticipates the collapse of the other horses: Dirck's mare Roos, with her 'quick wheeze', 'stretched neck and staggering knees', 'sunk tail, and horrible heave of the flank', sinks on her haunches at Hasselt.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary

title: Roos; the roan
short: Roos (Flemish 'rose') is Dirck's mare; Joris's horse is a 'roan', a coat of mixed white and coloured hairs.
body: The horses fall one by one. Roos sinks at Hasselt, and Joris promises 'We'll remember at Aix'. Joris's roan, just as Aix comes into sight, 'Rolled neck and croup over, lay dead as a stone'. The 'croup' is the rump of a horse. The suddenness of the death, in the middle of Joris's cry 'How they'll greet us!', is one of the poem's sharpest effects, and it leaves Roland 'to bear the whole weight / Of the news which alone could save Aix from her fate'.

title: the pitiless sun
short: The midday sun mocks the riders, and the dry stubble breaks under hooves like chaff.
body: The sun is now cloudless and cruel, an indifferent spectator. 'Brittle bright stubble like chaff' places the ride at harvest-time; the biblical image of chaff (e.g. Psalm 1:4, 'like the chaff which the wind driveth away') suggests worthlessness and dispersal, though Browning uses it chiefly for sound. The 'dome-spire' that 'sprang white' at Dalhem marks the first sight of the goal.

Bible (KJV), Psalm 1:4

title: buffcoat; holster; jack-boots
short: The rider strips off his leather coat, pistol-holsters, heavy boots and belt to lighten Roland's load.
body: A 'buffcoat' was a thick coat of buff leather (ox-hide) worn by soldiers in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; 'jack-boots' were heavy riding boots reaching above the knee; 'holsters' held pistols at the saddle. The details again point to the period of the Dutch Revolt or the Thirty Years' War. Shedding them, the rider stands in the stirrups and coaxes the horse with his 'pet-name', claps, laughs and sings, 'any noise, bad or good', in a desperate improvisation.

title: Aix
short: Aix-la-Chapelle (Aachen), Charlemagne's capital, now in western Germany; the news, whatever it was, saves the city.
body: Aachen, called Aix-la-Chapelle in French after Charlemagne's palace chapel, was the coronation city of German kings for centuries. 'Stood' is a deliberately flat, final verb: the horse has done all that can be done. The poem never tells us what the news was or from whom it came, which concentrates attention on the ride itself. Browning's refusal to supply history fits his comment that the poem has no historical incident behind it.

title: The ending: Roland's reward
short: The poem ends not with the news but with the horse, given the town's last wine 'by common consent' of its citizens.
body: The narrator remembers only friends flocking round and himself holding the horse's head between his knees, pouring wine down its throat. The 'burgesses' (citizens with civic rights) 'voted by common consent' that this was 'no more than his due'. The bureaucratic touch is gently comic, and the final word 'Ghent' completes the frame of the title. The 'last measure' is the riders' own last wine, given up for the horse. The poem's sympathy is for the horse; the riders' human motives remain vague.
